t.6.69.1: Hearing that terrible roar, whose sound was like the thunderbolt of Śakra, the bulls among the monkeys fled, looking about in all directions.
t.6.69.2: Then Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, spoke to all of them as they fled in different directions, dejected of face, wretched and terrified.
t.6.69.3: Why do you flee with downcast faces, O monkeys, having abandoned your zeal for battle? Where, then, has your valor gone?
t.6.69.4: Follow behind me as I go before you into battle, for it is not fitting for heroes endowed with noble lineage to turn back.
t.6.69.5: Thus addressed by the wise son of Vāyu, they, greatly enraged and yet glad at heart, seized mountain peaks and trees.
t.6.69.6: Roaring, the bull-like monkeys fell upon the Rākṣasas, and, surrounding Hanumān, they followed him in the great battle.
t.6.69.7: Surrounded on all sides by those foremost of the vānaras, Hanūmān, like a blazing fire, burned up the army of the enemy.
t.6.69.8: That very great monkey, surrounded by the army of vānaras and resembling Kāla, Antaka and Yama, wrought a slaughter of the rākṣasas.
t.6.69.9: But that great monkey Hanūmān, overcome by grief and by anger, hurled a huge rock upon the chariot of Rāvaṇi.
t.6.69.10: As soon as he saw it hurtling toward them, the charioteer then drove the chariot, yoked with obedient horses, far away.
t.6.69.11: Failing to reach Indrajit, who stood in his chariot together with his charioteer, that rock, raised in vain, split the earth and sank into it.
t.6.69.12: When the rock had fallen, the army of the Rākṣasas was shaken, and the forest-dwellers, roaring, rushed at him by the hundreds.
t.6.69.13: Those huge-bodied monkeys of fearsome valour, ready for battle, hurled trees and mountain peaks into the midst of their foes.
t.6.69.14: Struck down with trees by those mighty monkeys through their valour, the night-roaming demons of dreadful form writhed upon the field of battle.
t.6.69.15: Then Indrajit, seeing his own army harassed by the monkeys, seized his weapons and, enraged, went forth to face the enemy.
t.6.69.16: Surrounded by his own army and releasing floods of arrows, he, whose valour had been witnessed, slew a great many tigers among the monkeys.
t.6.69.17: And those monkeys, too, struck down his followers in battle with spears, thunderbolts, swords, paṭṭiśas and iron-headed maces.
t.6.69.18: With mighty sāla trees, trunks and branches and all, and with rocks, Hanumān wrought slaughter among the rākṣasas of terrible deeds.
t.6.69.19: Having held back the enemy army, Hanumān said to those forest-dwellers: "Turn back, all of you; this army is not to be overcome by us."
t.6.69.20: She for whose sake we fight, striving and casting aside our lives in our desire to do what is dear to Rāma, that daughter of Janaka has been slain.
t.6.69.21: Having made this matter known to Rāma and to Sugrīva, we shall do whatever those two shall decide in response.
t.6.69.22: Having spoken thus, that best of monkeys, restraining all the monkeys, slowly, slowly and unafraid, turned back together with his army.
t.6.69.23: But Indrajit, seeing Hanūmān going to where Rāghava was, betook himself to Nikumbhilā and made offerings into the fire.
t.6.69.24: Then on the sacrificial ground the fire, being offered oblations according to the rite by that Rākṣasa, blazed up, consuming the blood offered in the homa.
t.6.69.25: Wreathed in flames and gratified by the blood poured as oblation, that fierce fire blazed up and appeared like the sun come to the hour of twilight.
t.6.69.26: Then Indrajit, for the welfare of the rākṣasas, offered the oblation into the fire according to rule and in the prescribed manner; and seeing this, those rākṣasas, who knew what is prudent and what is imprudent, took their stand in great hosts.
